studies.title: The Mount And The Scroll
studies.meaning: Five oaths, and unlike the surah before them these all name specific things. The commentators identify the mount as the one where Moses received revelation, and they record several readings of the frequented House: a sanctuary in the heavens visited by angels, or the one in Mecca. The raised roof is the sky. What the list has in common is that each item is a place or object where revelation was given, written, or kept, so the oath is sworn on the machinery of scripture itself.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the classical ordering places this surah close to surah 51, which it answers in form: unnamed oaths there, named ones here. The commentators report no occasion for the individual oaths. They read the run of five as addressed to an audience that had books in view — Jewish and Christian scripture was known in the region — and that still treated the recitation being offered to them as something else entirely.

keyTerms.note: A passive participle from a root for a row or a line, the same root behind the word for a written line of text. It says the book is not just written but ruled, set out in order.
Fine skin prepared for writing, the most expensive surface available and the one used for texts meant to last. The following word says it is unrolled, so the writing is open rather than sealed.
From a root for inhabiting and for keeping a place in repair, which also gives the word for a lifespan. It describes a house that is continuously used, not merely standing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Parchment was wealth. A single prepared skin cost more than most people's daily earnings, and long texts represented herds. Mecca had few written documents; contracts and poetry lived in memory and were carried by professionals trained to hold them exactly. Someone swearing by a book on unrolled parchment was naming an object the audience associated with the settled communities to the north and with the scriptures those communities recited from.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase rendered as the frequented House occurs only in this ayah. It is one of the few Quranic expressions whose reference the classical commentators leave genuinely open, listing a heavenly sanctuary and the sanctuary at Mecca side by side, and al-Tabari records both without ruling between them. Nothing later in the surah returns to it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The oath objects are all witnesses to the fact that God has spoken before. A mountain where revelation came, a written scripture, a sanctuary attended, a sky held up: each is a point where the divine and the physical have already met. Swearing by them before announcing the punishment makes the announcement continuous with a record rather than a new claim, which is the surah's argument in miniature.

crossReferences.why: Swears by the same mountain alongside two other places, in another short Meccan oath sequence.
Describes the honoured pages the revelation is kept in, written by noble scribal hands.
Names the sky raised without visible pillars, the image behind the raised roof sworn by here.

studies.applyIt: Find something written that has outlasted its writer — a note in a family Quran, an inscription, a letter in a box. Hold it and notice that the words did not change while the person did. That gap is what this oath is pointing at. Then read a page of the Quran on paper rather than a screen, once, this week.

studies.title: Nothing Will Turn It Back
studies.meaning: The sixth oath is the strangest, a sea described with a word that classical readings split between filled to the brim and set alight, and the commentators keep both. Then the oath is answered in two short clauses: it is coming, and there is nothing that pushes it away. The description that follows moves the two most fixed things the audience knew. The sky rolls, and the mountains travel, so the vocabulary of solidity is handed over to motion.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The demand that the threatened punishment be produced on request is recorded repeatedly in this period, and this passage answers it by insisting on the certainty while giving no date. The commentators note that the surah's oaths and its verdict are separated by nothing: the reader arrives at the sentence immediately. No specific occasion is attached to these ayat.

keyTerms.note: A passive participle read in two ways by the early commentators, one from filling a basin and one from stoking an oven. Both readings are transmitted, and neither was abandoned in favour of the other.
An active participle from the verb for pushing something back. The sentence denies not the ability to stop the punishment but the existence of anyone in the role, which is a stronger denial.
A verb for a turning, rolling movement, used of smoke rising and of water disturbed in a container. It gives the sky the behaviour of a liquid rather than the collapse of a structure.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mountains were how you knew where you were. Routes across the peninsula were described by them, water was found at their feet, and tribes took their names from them. Nothing in that landscape was more permanent, and nothing was less likely to be described as travelling. The sea was the other fixed boundary, the edge past which trade went by ship and knowledge stopped. Both are named here and both are unsettled.
studies.didYouKnow: Two verbs in this passage are each reinforced by a bare noun from their own root placed immediately after: the sky sways a swaying, the mountains move a moving. Arabic uses the construction for emphasis, and the translation cannot carry it, so English versions render both simply as verbs and the doubling disappears.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes certainty and timing separate questions. It states that the punishment is coming and refuses to say when, and the refusal is not an evasion; it is the point. What is removed is the possibility of intervention, and the wording removes it by denying that any repeller exists at all. Then the description of the Day dissolves exactly the things a person would otherwise stand on.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same demand for the punishment by naming God as the one it comes from, with no date.
Describes mountains passing like clouds while you take them for solid, the same reversal.
Uses the other reading of the sea word, describing the seas set ablaze on that Day.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing in your life you treat as fixed — a job, a building, a body that has always worked. Say out loud that it is moveable. Not that it will move soon, only that it can. Most anxiety comes from mistaking things that are stable for things that are permanent, and this passage separates the two in six words.

studies.title: Playing At Deep Water
studies.meaning: The deniers are identified by an activity rather than by a belief. The word describes wading into something over your depth, and it is paired with a verb for playing, so what is condemned is treating serious matter as entertainment. The scene that follows is physical: they are shoved, and the verb is repeated as a noun to make the shoving emphatic. Then their own accusation is returned to them as a question, word for word.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The charge that the recitation was magic is recorded across the whole Meccan period and appears in the surah's later ayat as well. The commentators read the mockery described here as the gatherings where the message was discussed as a curiosity, since Mecca's leadership had social occasions in which the new preaching was a topic. No individual occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: Literally entering water and stirring it up. Used of talk, it means going into a subject you cannot handle and muddying it, which is why the Quran pairs it so often with falsehood.
A verb for pushing someone away roughly, used elsewhere of driving off an orphan who comes asking. The choice is pointed: the treatment they gave is the treatment described.
The question opens with the word they used, placed first for emphasis. It is not asking for information; it hands their own explanation back at the moment it can no longer be applied.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Evening talk was the entertainment. Men gathered after the day's work and traded news, poetry, genealogies and arguments, and a good session ran late. Reputation was made and lost in those circles, and a new claim was material for them long before it was a question anyone had to settle. The word used here for what the deniers were doing describes exactly that kind of talk: unhurried, communal, and going nowhere on purpose.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for shoving them into the Fire appears in only two places in the Quran. The other is a short Meccan surah where it describes a man pushing away an orphan who comes to him. The same physical action is attributed first to a person and then, on the Day, to what happens to that person.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats mockery as the substantive offence, not as a symptom of one. Nothing is said about arguments the deniers made, because the charge is that they made none: they played. What follows is a form of answer rather than a punishment alone, since the question put to them is exactly the one they were avoiding. And the return of their own word to them makes the scene an argument as much as a sentence.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb for shoving, of a man who drives away the orphan and neglects feeding the poor.
Puts the same word for idle plunging in the mouths of those asked why they entered the Fire.
Instructs turning away from people who plunge into mocking talk until they change the subject.

studies.applyIt: Think of one topic you discuss often and have never actually studied — a conflict, a doctrine, someone else's marriage. Notice how enjoyable the discussing is. This week, either read one serious thing about it or stop bringing it up. The passage is not against talk. It is against the specific pleasure of handling something serious as though nothing rests on it.

studies.title: Where Patience Changes Nothing
studies.meaning: One line, and it turns a familiar instruction inside out. Patience is offered and then cancelled in the same sentence: bear it or do not, the outcome is identical. The commentators read that cancelling as a definition rather than a taunt, since it says what endurance is for. Patience does its work where an outcome is still open, and here nothing is open. The closing clause supplies the reason: this is repayment, not a test.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a stretch of the surah addressed to those who treated the warning as a joke. The commentators observe that the wording quotes the ordinary Meccan and Arabian counsel to bear misfortune well, which was a genuine virtue in that culture and appears throughout its poetry. Here it is repeated in a place where it has nothing to purchase. No specific occasion is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: The imperative of the verb that names the central virtue of the Quran, from a root for binding something fast. Used here of people for whom the binding has no purpose left.
A noun for evenness, used of a flat road and of an equal share. It says the two options are level with each other, not that neither is possible, which is what makes the line severe.
From a root for settling an account and giving what is due. It is the same verb used of reward, so the word itself is neutral; only what is being settled decides the direction.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Bearing hardship without complaint was among the highest social virtues in Arabia, praised in the poetry alongside generosity and courage. A man who did not flinch under loss kept his standing whatever else happened, and the reputation was worth something concrete: alliances, marriages, credit. Telling such an audience that their endurance would buy nothing removed the one asset they were most confident they could carry anywhere.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran contains a second scene with almost this wording, where those being called to account say among themselves that it is the same whether they grieve or endure, since there is no refuge. There the sentence is spoken by the people themselves. Here it is spoken to them, which reverses who draws the conclusion.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah defines the limits of a virtue by removing its context. Patience is not treated as good in itself here; it is good because it holds a person steady while an outcome is still being decided. Where nothing is being decided, it becomes a posture with no object. That makes the Quran's repeated calls to patience arguments about time rather than about temperament, and it locates the value of endurance in what it is waiting for.

crossReferences.why: Puts nearly the same sentence in the mouths of those called to account, deciding it for themselves.
Gives the other side, where those who are patient receive their reward without any reckoning.
Shows patience doing its work in an open situation, attached to loss that is still being lived through.

studies.applyIt: The next time you are enduring something, ask what your patience is currently buying. Sometimes the honest answer is nothing, and the thing to do is act rather than bear. Patience is for what you cannot change while it is still being decided. Spend five minutes this week sorting one hardship into the right column, and then treat it accordingly.

studies.title: Couches Set In Rows
studies.meaning: The reward is described almost entirely in furniture and food, and the detail that carries the most weight is a single word about arrangement: the couches are in rows. Commentators read it as facing one another, so the picture is of a gathering rather than of separate pleasures. One clause interrupts the enjoyment to name what is absent, the punishment they were spared, which keeps the two outcomes in the same frame. The eating is then tied explicitly to what they did.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and set directly against the scene of the Fire two lines earlier, which is how this surah works throughout: the two futures alternate. The commentators note that the description uses the vocabulary of an Arabian feast and of the reception halls of the wealthier settled towns, so the imagery was concrete for the first audience rather than abstract. No occasion is reported for these ayat.

keyTerms.note: An active participle sharing a root with the word for fruit, and used of people in high spirits and easy conversation. It names a mood rather than an activity, which is why translations vary.
From the same root as the word for the God-conscious used at the start of the passage. The people described as guarding themselves are then described as guarded, and the repetition is deliberate.
A passive participle from the verb for lining up, used of ranks in prayer and of soldiers in formation. Applied to seating it implies an order, so nobody in the gathering is behind anyone else.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Seating was rank. At any Arabian gathering the order of places said who mattered, and disputes about it were real disputes. Guests reclined on cushions along the walls of a tent or a room, and where a man was put told him what his host thought of him. A description of couches set in rows, with everyone facing everyone, removed the whole apparatus by which status was displayed at a meal.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the God-conscious that opens this passage and the verb for shielding them a line later come from the same root. The people are named for what they guarded themselves against, and then God is described doing the guarding for them, using the same three letters. The English translation has to use two unrelated words.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage describes reward as relief and company before it describes pleasure. The clause about being shielded from the Fire sits inside the list of enjoyments, which means the absence of one outcome is itself counted among the goods of the other. And the food is explicitly attributed to what the people did, so the Quran does not present the garden as a gift disconnected from a life; it presents it as the same life continued into its consequences.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same seating, woven couches with people reclining on them facing one another.
Continues the picture with a cup that causes no headache and no loss of sense.
Repeats the phrase about eating and drinking in return for what was done in past days.

studies.applyIt: At your next meal with other people, change where everyone sits so that nobody has their back to anyone. It sounds trivial. The single word this passage spends on the couches is about arrangement, not comfort, and it is the only structural detail in four lines of description. Notice what a circle does to a conversation that a line does not.

studies.title: Joined To Their Children
studies.meaning: A promise about families with a limit attached in the same ayah. Descendants who followed in faith are brought up to the level of those before them, and the passage is careful about the accounting: nothing is taken from the parents to do it. The classical commentators emphasise both halves, because the raising is a gift and not a transfer. Then the ayah closes by restating individual responsibility in the strongest available terms, using the language of a pledge held against a debt.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The early community included households where some members believed and others did not, and where children followed parents into a faith that cost the family its standing. The commentators read the ayah against that setting without attaching it to a named incident. They note that the final clause was necessary precisely because the first part could otherwise be heard as inherited merit.

keyTerms.note: A causative from the verb for catching up with someone ahead of you. It puts the children behind at the start and moving forward, and the joining is done to them rather than earned by them.
A verb for reducing or withholding part of something owed. Its use here rules out the natural assumption that lifting one person must cost another, which is how human inheritance works.
The word for security lodged against a debt, held until the debt is settled. It makes each person the item deposited rather than the depositor, which is a sharper image than being merely responsible.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Pledges were how credit worked. A man borrowing against a future harvest left something of value with the lender — a weapon, a coat, sometimes an animal — and it stayed there, unusable, until the debt cleared. Everyone had seen a pledged item sitting in someone else's tent. Describing a person as the pledge, rather than as the one who lodged it, gave the audience an exact and uncomfortable picture.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a person held as a pledge appears in only two ayat of the Quran, here and in surah 74, where it takes the feminine form of the same term. This one states the principle for every person without exception; the other attaches one, for the companions of the right hand. Commentators read the pair together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah holds together two things that usually pull apart. Family matters, and the bond is not dissolved at the end; people are reunited and raised. And responsibility does not travel, so no one is carried by a parent's record. The reconciliation is in the accounting clause: the raising costs the higher party nothing, which means mercy is being added rather than redistributed. Justice and reunion are made compatible by increasing the total.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the pledge image and then attaches an exception, which this ayah states without one.
Names the same reunion, with parents, spouses and offspring entering the gardens together.
States the other half plainly: no bearer carries another's load, and a person has only what he worked for.

studies.applyIt: Say the name of one person in your family whose faith you would want to be standing next to at the end, and then do one thing for them this week that is not advice. A phone call, a debt paid, an hour of your time. The ayah promises reunion and then insists nobody rides on anyone. Both halves are worth acting on.

studies.title: They Turn And Ask
studies.meaning: The list of pleasures stops and something else begins. After the food and the cup, the passage names what is not in the cup — the loose talk and the wrongdoing that came with drinking in that world — and then the scene turns social. They face one another and start asking questions, and what comes out is memory. The first thing said in the garden, in this account, is about fear felt on earth, inside their own households.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The description of a cup carrying no idle speech and no wrongdoing addressed a specific social practice: drinking gatherings in Mecca were where quarrels started, oaths were made carelessly, and reputations were damaged. The commentators focus on what is denied rather than on what is offered. No occasion is reported; the passage continues the surah's alternating picture of the two outcomes.

keyTerms.note: Speech that carries no meaning and no consequence, including the oaths a person makes without intending them. Its absence is named as a feature of the drink, which locates the problem in the talk.
A passive participle for something stored away and protected, used of a pearl still in its shell. The point is unhandled freshness rather than concealment, so the comparison is about condition.
A participle for fear mixed with care, the feeling of someone worried about a person they love rather than about themselves. It is the Quran's word for a protective, anxious concern.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Pearls came up the Gulf coast and moved inland through the same caravans that carried everything else, and Arabs knew the trade well enough that the words for a pearl's condition were ordinary vocabulary. A pearl still shut in its shell had not been rubbed, drilled or strung. The comparison for the servers is not about beauty in general. It is about something that has not yet been used by anybody.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used for the people in the garden turning to question one another appears in the Quran describing both outcomes. The same construction is used of those in the Fire, who also face each other and ask, and of those in the garden. What differs is not the action but what the questioning finds when it looks back.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts conversation at the centre of the reward. What the people do with their perfected circumstances is turn to each other and talk, and the first subject is their earlier fear. That makes memory part of paradise rather than something erased by it. It also implies that the fear they carried was not wasted or shameful; it is recalled openly, in company, as part of the account of how they arrived.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same turning and questioning, and the conversation there recalls a companion who denied the resurrection.
Names the same absence, no idle talk and no lying, as a feature of that place.
Describes the same servers and the same cup that leaves no headache and no intoxication.

studies.applyIt: Ask someone close to you what they were most afraid of five years ago, and let them answer without adding your own version. The people in this passage begin their conversation there. Fear that has been survived becomes ordinary to talk about, and saying it out loud to another person is most of what makes it survivable in the first place.

studies.title: We Used To Call On Him
studies.meaning: The speakers finish their account of themselves with one sentence about their past, and it is not about deeds. They used to call on Him. The verb is the ordinary one for asking, and it is placed as the whole explanation of how they arrived. Two names follow, one of them rare. Then the surah turns without a pause to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and answers the labels being thrown at him, beginning with the two his opponents used most.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Soothsayer, madman and poet were the three explanations Mecca offered for the recitation, and the sources report them being tried in turn, since each accounted for unusual speech in a way the audience recognised. This passage answers all three in two lines. The last of them comes with a wish attached: that time would deal with the man and the problem would resolve itself.

keyTerms.note: A hot wind that enters through the pores, named from the word for a small opening. It is the desert's specific killer, and the Quran uses it for the heat of the punishment.
From a root for wide open land and for dutiful goodness, the same root behind the word for kindness to parents. As a divine name it appears here and nowhere else in the Quran.
A word the commentators gloss as death and as the turning of the days that wears things out. What the opponents were awaiting was not an event they would cause but one they expected.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A poet was a public institution, not a private artist. Tribes kept them, and a poet's satire could damage a rival tribe's standing for a generation. Poets were also believed to be attended by a familiar spirit, which is why calling someone a poet, a soothsayer and a madman were versions of one accusation: that the speech came from somewhere other than the speaker. All three explained the effect without accepting the source.
studies.didYouKnow: The name given to God at the end of this passage, usually rendered the Kind or the Benevolent, is used of God in only this one ayah of the Quran. Its root is the same one that supplies the ordinary word for dutiful kindness shown to a parent, so the name comes from the vocabulary of family obligation rather than of power.
studies.theologicalSignificance: What the saved people offer as their record is a habit of asking, not a list of achievements. The Quran lets that stand as sufficient, which places relationship before accomplishment in the account of a life. The divine name that follows explains why: kindness of the kind owed within a family, not the favour of a distant power. Then the instruction to keep reminding is grounded in the same thing, described as a favour rather than a duty.

crossReferences.why: Denies the same two labels for the recitation, poet and soothsayer, in almost the same order.
States that calling on God is answered, which is the practice these people name as their record.
Uses the same word for the scorching wind in another description of the punishment.

studies.applyIt: Notice how you talk to God when nothing is wrong. Most people only have a vocabulary for asking under pressure. The people in this passage describe an ordinary, continued habit of calling on Him, and it is the only thing they say about their past. Ask for one small thing today that you would normally not bother mentioning.

studies.title: Then Bring One Like It
studies.meaning: The reply to the wish that time would remove him is one word: wait. He joins them in it, which turns their threat into a shared position. Then the questions begin, and the second one is unusual because it takes the opponents seriously as thinkers before dismissing them. Their minds are asked about. The answer given is not that they reasoned badly but that they did not believe, and the challenge that follows asks for a text rather than an argument.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Mecca's leadership included men known for judgement and sound counsel, and the word used here for their minds is the one their culture applied to exactly that quality. The challenge to produce something comparable appears several times in the Quran at different scales, from a single surah upward. Here the demand is for a discourse, the broadest form of it, and no occasion is reported for the ayah.

keyTerms.note: A plural whose singular covers both a dream and settled good sense, the quality of a man who does not act rashly. Arabic keeps the two meanings in one word, and commentators note both here.
A verb form that means to fabricate speech and attribute it to someone else. It is not the ordinary word for saying; the form itself carries the accusation of invention.
The ordinary word for talk or a report, not a term for scripture. Asking for a discourse like it sets the bar at the level of speech itself rather than at content or claim.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia judged people by speech. Annual gatherings included recitation contests, and a tribe's standing could rise on the strength of one poet. Composition was a competitive public skill with recognised experts and an audience trained to hear a false line. Challenging that audience to match a text was not an abstract dare. It was an invitation into the one arena in which they believed themselves unbeatable.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah fires off a run of questions all opening with the same short Arabic particle. It occurs fifteen times between its thirtieth and forty-third ayat, twelve of them at the head of an ayah, and nine of those ayat follow one another without a break. The drumming effect is lost in translation, which has to vary the wording.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage locates unbelief below the level of reasoning. It asks whether the opponents' judgement requires their position, and answers that it does not; then it asks whether they think the text was invented, and answers that the real state is simply that they do not believe. That order matters. Argument is treated as a report of a prior disposition rather than its cause, which is why the response offered is a test anyone can run rather than a further argument.

crossReferences.why: Sets the same challenge at the scale of a single surah, and says it will not be met.
Widens the challenge to humans and jinn together, and says they could not do it even helping each other.
Asks for ten invented surahs like it, a middle step between the two other versions.

studies.applyIt: Think of a position you hold that you have never actually tested, and design the smallest test you could run this week. Not a debate, a check. The passage answers a claim by proposing something the other side could simply do. Most disagreements never reach that point, and reaching it usually tells you which side is doing the reasoning.

studies.title: Created From Nothing, Or Creators
studies.meaning: Three questions with no middle ground offered, and they work by elimination. Either you came from nothing, with no cause at all, or you made yourself, or somebody made you: the third option is left unstated because the first two are unavailable. The same structure is then applied to the heavens and the earth and to the storehouses of provision. The verdict inserted halfway through is not that they are wrong but that they lack certainty.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. A well-attested report describes a leading Meccan, then still opposed to the message, hearing these ayat recited in a prayer some years later and saying afterwards that his heart was close to flying. He had travelled north on unrelated business. The report is transmitted in the major classical collections, and the commentators cite it when discussing the argumentative force of this particular passage.

keyTerms.note: A phrase read two ways by the commentators: created by no maker at all, or created out of no material. Both readings leave the questioner with the same unusable answer.
From a root for knowledge that has settled and stopped moving, the opposite of doubt rather than of ignorance. The charge is not that they know nothing but that nothing has become firm.
The plural of a word for a locked store where grain and valuables were kept against a bad year. Applied to God it names the reserves from which provision is released, not a hoard.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Every settled household had a store. Grain, dates and oil were kept sealed against the season when nothing grew, and the man who held the key held real power over the people who ate from it. In a bad year a storehouse decided who survived. Asking whether the opponents held God's storehouses was asking whether they controlled the rain, the harvest and the caravan, which was a question with an obvious answer.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a controller at the end of this passage is written in the standard Uthmani text with an unusual spelling, and the classical reciters transmit more than one pronunciation of one of its letters. It is one of a small number of words in the Quran where the received readings preserve a recognised variation in a single letter.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The argument does not try to prove God exists. It removes the alternatives and leaves the audience holding a conclusion they already have. What it establishes is that the question of origin is not optional: everyone answers it, including by refusing to. The diagnosis inserted in the middle then shifts the ground from knowledge to certainty, which is a claim about the state of a person rather than about the state of an argument.

crossReferences.why: Asks the same question about the reader's own making, narrowing it to the moment of conception.
Names the keys of the unseen as God's alone, the same storehouse image from the other side.
States that the storehouses of everything are with God and are released in a known measure.

studies.applyIt: Sit with the first question for one minute without reaching for an answer you already have. You were not there when you began. Somebody or something started you, and you have no memory of it and no say in it. That is not an argument you need to win. It is a fact about your position that most days you manage never to notice.

studies.title: A Ladder To The Sky
studies.meaning: The questioning continues and turns to sources. If they claim knowledge nobody else has, where did it come from: is there a ladder, and did someone climb it and listen? The demand that follows is for evidence anyone could inspect. Then three more possibilities are eliminated in a line each: an arrangement about children that would be insulting if applied to them, a financial motive on the messenger's side, and private access to the future.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Some Arabian groups described certain of their deities as God's daughters, while the birth of a daughter was treated in the same society as a misfortune, and the Quran repeatedly puts those two facts next to each other. The question about payment reflects the ordinary suspicion of a preacher's motives, and the sources record that no fee was ever asked. No specific occasion is reported.

keyTerms.note: An ordinary household object, from a root for safety and for climbing without falling. The question makes access to the unseen a matter of equipment, which is exactly what it cannot be.
A payment owed that brings no benefit back, used of a penalty and of a loss a person is stuck with. It names the burden rather than the sum, so the question is about resentment.
What is absent from perception, not what is mysterious. The following clause makes the test practical: if they had it, they would be writing it down, as any merchant records what he knows.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Writing existed in Mecca and was used for exactly one thing: keeping accounts. Merchants recorded debts, shares and delivery dates because memory was not trusted with numbers, and a written record settled disputes. So the image of people writing down the unseen is a commercial one. It asks whether they have information worth booking, and it treats the absence of any ledger as the answer.
studies.didYouKnow: The ladder in this ayah is one of only two places the Quran uses the word, and the other also appears in a challenge about reaching the sky for information. In both cases the object named is deliberately mundane, so the impossibility is expressed through a piece of ordinary equipment rather than through grand language.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a standard for religious claims and applies it to both sides. Anyone asserting knowledge of what cannot be seen is asked where it came from, and a claim with no traceable source is treated as no claim at all. The demand for a clear authority is not a rhetorical flourish; it is the same standard the Quran repeatedly asks of itself. What is being refused is not disagreement but assertion without account.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same ladder image, of seeking a sign by climbing into the sky.
Sets the attribution of daughters to God beside the shame felt at a daughter's birth.
Answers the payment question directly: whatever reward was asked for is returned, since the payment comes from God.

studies.applyIt: The next time someone tells you something confidently about the future — markets, a relationship, a diagnosis — ask them, kindly, how they know. Not to catch them out. Half the time the answer is a real source and you have learned something. The other half, the question is the most useful thing in the conversation, and it works on your own claims too.

studies.title: They Would Call It Cloud
studies.meaning: The last two questions close the sequence and then the passage does something different. It stops asking and describes what would happen if the sign they keep demanding actually arrived: a piece of the sky falling, and an explanation ready immediately. Piled clouds. The commentators read this as the answer to every request for a miracle, since the request was never about evidence. The instruction that follows is to leave them, which is not abandonment but the end of arguing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Demands for a visible sign are recorded throughout this period, including a request that a piece of the sky be dropped on the community as proof. The commentators connect this ayah to that demand directly. The plotting mentioned just before is read against the organised opposition in Mecca, which by this stage involved coordination rather than individual hostility.

keyTerms.note: A passive participle from the verb for scheming, so the plotters are named as the targets. The line reverses the grammar of the previous clause without changing the word.
A broken-off portion of something larger, used of a piece of cloth and of a shard. It is the exact word the opponents themselves used when demanding that the sky be dropped on them.
A passive participle for something stacked in layers, used of clouds banked before rain. The word makes their explanation a technically competent one, which is what makes the scene devastating.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reading the sky was a survival skill. A herder or a caravan master could tell a rain cloud from a dust haze at distance, name the layers, and judge how long he had. The vocabulary was precise because getting it wrong cost animals or lives. So the answer put in the opponents' mouths is not stupidity. It is expertise, applied confidently to the one thing it does not fit.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for a fragment of the sky is the same one the Meccan opponents used elsewhere in the Quran when they demanded that the sky be brought down on them in pieces. The surah quotes their own demand back into a hypothetical, and then supplies the explanation they would reach for if it were granted.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage denies that evidence is the obstacle. A sign large enough to end the argument is imagined and then absorbed by an ordinary explanation, which means the capacity to explain away is unlimited. That reframes belief as something other than a conclusion from data. The instruction to leave them follows logically rather than bitterly: if the problem is not information, then supplying more of it is not the remedy.

crossReferences.why: Lists the signs the opponents demanded, including bringing down the sky on them in pieces.
Says that even a gate opened in the sky would be explained as eyes bewitched.
States that a scheme recoils on the people who make it, the reversal used here.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you explain away something that does not fit what you already think. Everyone does it, and it feels exactly like reasoning. Give it a name when you catch it — say to yourself, that was a piled cloud — and then sit with the thing you explained away for another minute before deciding. One minute is usually enough to tell the difference.

studies.title: A Punishment Before That
studies.meaning: Two lines that close the argument by narrowing the timeframe. First the plotting is followed to its end and found empty, with no help arriving from any direction. Then a second punishment is named, and the phrase used places it earlier than the Day. Commentators read it variously as loss in this life, as defeat, or as what comes in the grave, and they record the range. The last clause says the people it applies to are unaware of it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the commentators note that some of them read the nearer punishment as the defeat the Meccan leadership later suffered, which would make the line a prediction. Others keep it general. The surah has just told the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to leave them until their Day, and these two lines qualify that: leaving them is not the same as nothing happening in the meantime.

keyTerms.note: From a root for wealth and for having enough. The verb asks not whether the plotting works but whether it covers anything, which is the language of a bill that falls short.
A preposition of position that can mean beneath, nearer than, or other than. The commentators split accordingly, and the range of readings about this punishment follows directly from that ambiguity.
The plain verb for knowing, in the present tense, so the ignorance is ongoing rather than final. It leaves open the possibility that they might come to know, which the surah does not close off.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Protection was the basic unit of security. A man belonged to a clan and the clan answered for him, so the standard threat was not death but exposure: losing the people who would come when you called. Everyone had seen someone put outside that arrangement. Saying that no help would arrive on that Day named the specific terror of the society, which was not pain but being unbacked.
studies.didYouKnow: The root for plotting appears three times in five lines of this surah: as what the opponents intend, as a passive naming them the ones plotted against, and as the thing that will not cover their costs on the Day. One root carries the whole reversal, and the English translation needs three different phrasings to follow it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts a limit on how much of the consequence is postponed. Naming a punishment that comes before the Day answers a specific complaint, that the wicked prosper and nothing happens, without turning every misfortune into a verdict. And the final clause is careful: the people concerned do not know about it, which means the passage is not inviting anyone to identify it in someone else's life. It states that the accounting has already begun.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase for a nearer punishment given before the greater one, so that people may return.
Shows a nearer punishment falling on Pharaoh's people before the greater one is named.
Warns against being impressed by the movement of the disbelievers through the land, a brief enjoyment.

studies.applyIt: If you are carrying a grievance about someone who seems to be getting away with something, notice how much of your energy goes into wanting the timing changed rather than the outcome. This passage says some of the account is already being settled and that you are not in a position to see it. Put the file down for a week and see what you get back.

studies.title: You Are Before Our Eyes
studies.meaning: The surah ends by giving one instruction and one reason. The instruction is to wait, and the reason is a phrase that has no obvious English equivalent: you are in Our eyes. Commentators read it as under God's watch, protection and care at once, and they do not separate the three. Then the waiting is filled. Three times are named — on rising, part of the night, and the hour when the stars fade — so patience is given something to do.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and these are the surah's closing lines. The commentators differ over what the phrase about rising refers to: standing for prayer, rising from sleep, rising from a gathering, or getting up from any seat. They record the range without settling it, and the breadth is part of why the ayah is quoted so often. No occasion is reported for either line.

keyTerms.note: A plural of the word for an eye, with a preposition that means within or in the presence of. Classical commentators read it as care and watchfulness together, and they insist it implies nothing bodily.
From a root for swimming and moving freely through something, so declaring God's perfection is described with a verb of motion. It means removing every defect from the idea, not adding praise to it.
A noun for turning the back and withdrawing, used of an army in retreat. Applied to the stars it names the moment they go out at dawn, the hand-over between night and day.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The night sky was a clock and a map. Travellers moved after dark to avoid the heat and steered by named stars, and the point at which those stars washed out told everyone the night was over and the day's obligations had started. Nobody needed an instrument. The moment the passage names as a time for remembrance is the one moment in the day that every person in that society could identify without being told.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah opens by swearing on a mountain, a book, a sanctuary, a sky and a sea, and closes by asking for a few words said at three ordinary moments of a day. Nothing in between narrows the gap. The shape is deliberate: an argument at cosmic scale that ends with an instruction small enough for anyone to carry out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reason given for patience is not that the wait is short or that the outcome is good. It is that the one waiting is seen. That relocates endurance from a calculation about the future to a fact about the present, which is a different kind of consolation and a more durable one. And the practice attached to it is not petition but glorification, so the waiting is filled with something that asks for nothing.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase, telling Noah to build the ark before God's eyes and under instruction.
Names the same times for glorification, before sunrise and sunset and part of the night.
Gives the same closing pattern, patience for the decision of your Lord followed by night remembrance.

studies.applyIt: Take the third of the times this passage names and use it once this week. Set an alarm for the last part of the night, get up, and say a few words of praise before the sky lightens, then go back to sleep. It does not need to be long. The point is to have been awake in the one hour nobody else is watching you.
